description: Per-sound comparison of the three reading settings the app uses, plus an 'also exists' list. Plain-English values were written for ALEF as paraphrases of the sources named in sources.json. No native speaker or linguist has reviewed this file.

confidence.high: Two or more of the pages we read agree on the Israeli and Ashkenazi cells and on the 'other communities' cell.
confidence.medium: One page supports it, or the pages agree on the substance but differ in detail.
confidence.low: Mostly the project's own inference, or the page itself flags the claim as weak.

settings.israeli: Modern Israeli: the everyday standard Hebrew of Israel. ALEF makes no claim about Tel Aviv-specific speech; no source for it was found.
settings.american: American synagogue (the app's 'sephardi' setting): Sephardi/Israeli vowel values said with American-English habits. This is a teaching convention in ALEF, not a community with one fixed accent.
settings.ashkenazi: Traditional Ashkenazi liturgical reading. Real Ashkenazi Hebrew has regional dialects (Lithuanian, Polish, German, Hungarian, ...); ALEF picks the commonest siddur values.
settings.sephardi: Traditional Sephardi reading, as kept in Sephardi and Mizrahi communities: the sounds behind the app's Sephardi-values setting. Spellings in this column follow the SephardicU transliteration guide, which gives each Hebrew letter one Latin letter or pair.

sounds.label: Tav without a dot (ת)
sounds.american: t in most non-Orthodox practice (Shabbat). Orthodox and Ashkenazi-leaning synagogues often say s (Shabbos).

other.who: Yemenite, Iraqi and some Greek communities
other.say: th as in thin
d, or th as in this

sounds.americanBasis: Benor and Cohen show Reform and Conservative respondents leaning to the Israeli form of one word; the rest is lane 3's inference.
sounds.note: A tav WITH a dot (dagesh) is t in every tradition listed here. The single most audible switch between Ashkenazi and the others.

sephardi.say: t (Shabat). A few communities keep a soft th.
sephardi.translit: t; th where the soft form is kept

sounds.label: Kamatz (T-shaped mark)
sounds.american: ah, as in father. Some older or Orthodox speakers say aw.
sounds.ashkenazi: o or aw (Borukh). Southern Ashkenazi dialects use u when the syllable is open.

other.say: ah, the same as patach
a back, rounded vowel like the Ashkenazi o (per the Ashkenazi Hebrew page)

sounds.americanBasis: lane 3 inference; the aw habit is described in data/pronunciation/niqqud.json without an outside source.
sounds.note: Kamatz katan (a short o in a few words such as kol) is a separate topic that ALEF handles only for a short word list; it is not covered here.

sephardi.say: ah, like patach (barukh). Kamatz katan is read o by the sound of the word, not by the grammar books: kal, tsahorayim.

sounds.label: Patach and kamatz: same vowel or two?
sounds.ashkenazi: Two vowels: patach is ah, kamatz is o or aw.

other.say: Same: both ah. The page adds that formal liturgical reading often restores a distinction (it does not say how).
Kept apart; patach and segol sound alike

sounds.americanBasis: Follows the Israeli/Sephardi value in the app's CONTRACT; lane 3 inference for actual American speech.
sounds.note: This merger is why Israeli recordings and Sephardi-values readings agree on every kamatz and patach.

sephardi.say: Same vowel: both ah. A formal reader may hold the kamatz a little longer.

sounds.label: Cholam (dot above)
sounds.ashkenazi: varies by region: oh (southern German), oy (Polish/Galician), ey (Lithuanian), ow (northern German). The app's siddur style writes plain o.

other.say: oh

sounds.note: Chabad.org describes the oy, ay and ow versions as Yiddish-influenced and not official.

sephardi.say: o, a plain o, never oy or au (Torah, Shalom).

sounds.label: Tsere (two dots) and segol (three dots)
sounds.israeli: eh, as in bed. Some speakers say ey in some words.
sounds.american: eh, often stretched into an ay glide (HAY-nu).
sounds.ashkenazi: ey, as in they (some Polish usage: ai)

other.say: eh; tsere and segol sound the same

sounds.americanBasis: The glide is lane 3's own observation in prayerwords.json; unreviewed.

sephardi.say: e, a plain e, never ey (Shema, Amen).

sounds.label: Shva (two dots, stacked)
sounds.israeli: a quick e, or nothing at all in everyday speech
sounds.american: a quick e when reading prayers
sounds.ashkenazi: often dropped in speech; read as a short e or uh when reading liturgy strictly

other.say: a short e in every position where it is sounded; always sounded after a long vowel

sounds.note: The Ashkenazi cell comes from lane 3's data only; the fetched pages describe dropping the vocal shva as an Ashkenazi feature that entered Israeli speech. Rules for WHICH shvas are sounded are in src/pronunciation/shva.js and are partly TODO.

sephardi.say: e where it is vocal, and it is sounded, not swallowed (Berakhah).

sounds.label: Ayin (ע)
sounds.israeli: silent, or a tiny catch like the break in uh-oh (same as alef)
sounds.ashkenazi: silent in most forms. Traditional authorities advised a throaty sound in prayer, which is rarely done.

other.who: Balkan, Anatolian, North African and Levantine Sephardim
other.say: a throaty, Arabic-like pharyngeal sound
the same pharyngeal sound
sometimes keep it, less often than het
an ng sound as in singing

sounds.americanBasis: Same as Israeli; lane 3 inference for American habits.
sounds.note: In Israeli speech ayin and alef are the same sound. Trying a pharyngeal there is likely to sound foreign; that last point is lane 3's inference.

sephardi.say: A real sound from the throat, like the Arabic ayin, among Balkan, Turkish, North African and Levantine Sephardim; the Spanish-Portuguese and Italian communities say ng as in singing.
sephardi.translit: ’ (an apostrophe: Shema’, ma’ariv); ng among Western Sephardim

sounds.label: Chet (ח) versus khaf (כ without dot)
sounds.israeli: ch as in Scottish loch, the same sound as khaf
sounds.american: ch as in Bach for both (the usual habit); some say a plain h, which is a slip to fix
sounds.ashkenazi: ch as in Bach, the same as khaf. A throaty sound was advised but is rarely heard.

other.who: Sephardim and Mizrahim who keep it, and Yemenite
other.say: a pharyngeal, throaty h that differs from khaf
often keep the pharyngeal

sephardi.say: A breathy h from the throat, kept apart from khaf.

sounds.label: Qof (ק)
sounds.israeli: k, the same as kaf with a dot

other.say: k
kept distinct from kaf with a dot, as in Arabic

sounds.note: A deeper qof in some Mizrahi communities is plausible but the pages we read name only Georgian Jews, so ALEF names only them.

sephardi.say: k for almost everyone; a few communities keep a deeper k.
sephardi.translit: q, so that it stays apart from kaf (k)

sounds.label: Resh (ר)
sounds.israeli: a back-of-the-throat r, like French or German; nearly all Israeli Jews use it
sounds.american: the English r (most Americans). Hearing a uvular r in Israel is normal; using the English r is a common marker of a foreign speaker (lane 3's inference).
sounds.ashkenazi: a tapped or trilled r or a uvular r, depending on region

other.say: a front tapped or trilled r, like Spanish
often keep the trilled r

sounds.note: This is a place where an Israeli recording is NOT a good model for 'Sephardi' sounds: the Israeli r and the Sephardi r differ.

sephardi.say: A tapped or trilled r at the front of the mouth, like Spanish r.

sounds.label: Which syllable is stressed
sounds.israeli: most words on the last syllable; some, such as words of the melech/boker type, on the one before; spoken Israeli drifts toward the second-to-last syllable
sounds.american: last syllable in prayer words (baRUKH, shaLOM), as in Israeli
sounds.ashkenazi: traditionally the second-to-last syllable (SHOlom, BOrukh), but final stress was promoted for Torah reading and public prayer, and many congregations use it

other.say: keeps the older pattern, which for most words is the last syllable
the Wikipedia page says second-to-last, but tags that claim 'citation needed'; ALEF does not rely on it

sounds.note: The Chabad page does not discuss stress. The Sephardi Wikipedia page says only that stress is final where Biblical Hebrew puts it there.

sephardi.say: On the last syllable wherever the Bible puts it there, which is most words (shaBAT, baRUKH).
sephardi.translit: no mark in the spelling; the ai diphthong is written ai

claims: Pharyngeal het and ayin, as in Arabic.
Gimel without a dot is a voiced throat fricative and with a dot is a j sound.
Tav without a dot is th as in thin; dalet without a dot is th as in this.
alsoExists.note: Described by one Wikipedia article only (first 100,000 of 124,343 characters read). ALEF has no Yemenite audio, respelling or lesson; this is a note that it exists.

alsoExists.who: Mizrahi and Sephardi communities (Middle East, North Africa, Balkans, Anatolia)
claims: Many keep pharyngeal het and sometimes ayin; the details differ by community.
Some read tav as th, and some keep qof distinct (the pages we read name Iraqi, Greek and Georgian examples).
There is no single 'Sephardi accent': the pages stress many variants inside each grouping.
alsoExists.note: ALEF's 'sephardi' setting is NOT a model of any of these communities. If your synagogue belongs to one, ask a member or the cantor and treat this app as a general guide only.

claims: Bet without a dot traditionally between b and v, a habit that is declining.
